name: Ledger of the Unnamed
description:
Released in 2201 by Cassian Pale & The Redline Choir offshoot project Ferrous Saints under a pirate neural feed imprint, 'Ledger of the Unnamed' became the defining protest anthem of the post-Compact Riots era. Built on a foundation of Igbo call-and-response vocals, Scandinavian drone bass, and a relentless taiko-derived percussion loop, the song catalogs the deaths of 214 Shelf workers whose fatalities were administratively erased from Vantablack Media's labor casualty reports following the Crucible Platform collapse of 2200. The lyrics are stark and repetitive in the tradition of worker laments — each verse names a category of death (crush, exposure, debt seizure, erasure) before the chorus erupts with the demand: 'Write us in, write us in, or burn the whole book down.'
The song was banned within seventy-two hours of its initial pirate broadcast, but by then it had already been copied to an estimated forty thousand personal neural caches across the Shelf and Circuit. It is sung at funerals, spray-painted in fragments on tunnel walls, and played at the start of every unofficial labor action in Meridian 88's maintenance sector. Vantablack Media has attempted three times to release sanitized cover versions — each effort was met with organized silence campaigns and physical destruction of promotional kiosks.
creator: Ferrous Saints
audience: Shelf workers, Circuit labor organizers, union remnants, political underground, maintenance crews, dock workers
cultural_impact: More than any single piece of media in a generation, 'Ledger of the Unnamed' forced the concept of administrative erasure into popular consciousness. Graffiti versions of its chorus appear on infrastructure walls from the lowest Shelf sub-levels to mid-Circuit transit corridors. Corporate security has standing orders to silence any public broadcast of the song, which has paradoxically made hearing it — even a few bars drifting from a cracked window — a symbol of resistance and solidarity. The song is credited by labor historians as a catalyst for the 2203 Maintenance Compact negotiations.
story_hooks: A player character discovers their deceased parent is one of the 214 names the song was written about — but the song lists a death circumstance that contradicts the official family story.
A Vantablack Media compliance officer is tasked with locating the original neural-feed master recording and destroying it — but has begun privately listening to it on loop.
A Shelf funeral is interrupted by corporate security claiming the playing of the song constitutes an illegal assembly — the mourners must decide whether to disperse or stand.
